guideTitle: 6 Best Emergency Lights for Power Outages in 2026
metaTitle: Best Emergency Lights for Power Outages (2026)
metaDescription: Six outage lights compared: plug-in auto-on lights, emergency bulbs and battery lanterns, with notes on brightness, runtime, power source and where to use each.
introParagraphs: A power outage rarely arrives at a convenient time. The lights drop in the hallway, the stairs vanish, and the phone flashlight is somewhere in the other room. The best preparation is not one flashlight in a drawer but a small set of lights that cover the first seconds, the walk to the bathroom and the long evening that follows. Different tools fit each of those moments, and this guide compares six that do.

Three styles appear in the lineup. The ROSSEX and Energizer plug into a wall outlet, charge quietly and switch on by themselves when the power fails. The DEBAOBULB and BoRccdit are rechargeable bulbs that screw into an ordinary socket and keep glowing after the mains drop. The Consciot and Etekcity are battery powered lanterns that you carry from room to room. Each style solves a slightly different problem, so most households do best with two of the three.

We evaluated each pick from product specifications and buyer feedback patterns, not from lab work. We looked at how the light turns on, what powers it, the brightness and runtime figures the listing gives, and how awkward it would be to use at night with a tired eye. All brightness and runtime figures here are the makers' claims, and none of these should be treated as code compliant exit lighting unless a listing explicitly says so.

products.name: Energizer Weatheready Auto-On LED Light 3-Pack
products.description:
The Energizer is the straightforward way to set up automatic outage lighting. Each of the three units plugs into a standard outlet, keeps itself charged and turns on when the power fails. Lift it out of the wall and it becomes a compact handheld flashlight, so the same piece covers the first moment of an outage and the walk across the room.

The tradeoff is that the listing gives no brightness or runtime figures in the details we saw. It is therefore best treated as a guide light for hallways and stairs, not a room light. A plug-in unit also takes up an outlet or half of one, which matters in older homes with few sockets. Check that it does not block the second plug of a duplex outlet.

In ownership terms, it is a set and forget device. You plug it in and it stays put, and a quick check every few months confirms it still lights. Compared with the ROSSEX it is a simpler, branded alternative, and compared with a lantern it needs no batteries. It is the pick for the first thing you want to happen when the lights go out.
products.bestFor: Hallways, stairs and bedrooms where a light must come on without you touching it.
pros: Switches on by itself when power fails
cons: No brightness figures in the listing
Small light, not for a whole room

products.name: ROSSEX 4-in-1 Plug-In Emergency Light
products.description:
The ROSSEX does more than one job. It switches on automatically during an outage, recharges from a standard socket through its built-in lithium battery, and doubles as a normal flashlight and a nightlight. The listing calls it 4 in 1, and it is sold in packs of three, four and six, which makes it easy to cover a whole floor.

The tradeoff is that the extra modes can be confusing for some users. A nightlight that is also an emergency light needs the right switch setting to behave correctly, so it is worth reading the instructions once. The listing does not give lumen or runtime figures in the details we saw, so brightness is unknown.

For ownership, the multi pack is the advantage. You can place one in every hallway and bathroom and still have spares for a handheld. Compared with the Energizer it has more modes, and compared with the bulbs it needs no socket. It is a good value if you want one light that is a nightlight every day and an emergency light once in a while.
products.bestFor: Whole-home coverage with one light that doubles as a nightlight.
pros: Sold in packs of three to six
cons: Modes need a quick read of instructions

products.name: DEBAOBULB Rechargeable Emergency Light Bulb 6-Pack
products.description:
The DEBAOBULB turns any lamp or ceiling fixture into an outage light. These are standard E26 bulbs rated at 9 watts, with 800 lumens on mains power and a 6000K daylight color. The listing says they work like a regular bulb and recharge themselves, then keep glowing when the power drops, so there is nothing to plug in and nothing new to remember.

The tradeoff is that daylight color is cool and bright, which some people find harsh in a bedroom. A bulb also depends on the fixture: it only glows if the switch is on, and a wall switch left off will keep it dark. The listing does not give backup runtime in the details we saw, so we cannot say how long it lasts after the outage begins.

For ownership, six bulbs cover a lot of fixtures, and they can stay in place for years. Compared with the BoRccdit they offer a clear mains lumen figure but no stated backup duration, and compared with plug-in lights they light a whole room. They suit people who would rather change a bulb than add a device.
products.bestFor: Living rooms and kitchens where you want room lighting from an existing fixture.
cons: Cool daylight color is harsh at night

products.name: BoRccdit KeepLit Rechargeable Emergency Bulb 8-Pack
products.description:
The BoRccdit KeepLit leads with backup duration. The listing claims up to 48 hours of lighting and offers three brightness levels at 10, 50 and 100 percent, so you can stretch the battery by dimming. It is a standard A19 bulb with an E26 or E27 base and a 12 watt rating that works like any bulb when the mains is on.

The tradeoff is that 48 hours is a maker's claim, and it presumably applies to the lowest level. Running at 100 percent will drain far faster. Eight bulbs is also a big pack, which is excellent for a large home but more than a small apartment needs. As with all bulb based systems, the light stays dark if the switch is off.

For ownership, the brightness steps are the real feature, because you can dim all the bulbs during a long outage. Compared with the DEBAOBULB it gives a stated backup claim and dimming, while the DEBAOBULB gives a mains lumen figure. It is the right pick for areas with long outages, such as snow or hurricane regions.
products.bestFor: Regions with long outages where dimming and a large backup claim matter.
pros: Three brightness levels to stretch power
Eight bulbs cover a large home
cons: Runtime figure is the maker's claim
Eight-pack is more than many need
Dark if the switch is off

products.name: Consciot 1000LM Battery-Powered LED Lantern
products.description:
The Consciot is the brightest lantern here on paper. The listing claims up to 1000 lumens in a 360 degree glow, with four modes: cool white, warm white, combined white and strobe. It runs on three D cell batteries, which are not included, and carries an IPX4 splash resistance rating that makes it suitable for a porch or a storm.

The tradeoff is battery logistics. Three D cells are bulky and expensive to keep stocked, and a lantern is only useful if you have fresh ones. A strobe mode is not something most households need. The 1000 lumen figure is a maker claim, so treat it as a comparison point.

For ownership, the lantern sits in a closet and comes out on demand. Compared with the Etekcity it offers far more claimed light but at the cost of D cell batteries, and compared with plug in lights it lights a room. It suits a family room or a kitchen table during a long outage.
products.bestFor: Lighting a family room or kitchen table during a long outage.

products.name: Etekcity LED Collapsible Lantern 2-Pack
products.description:
The Etekcity is a collapsible lantern that packs flat. It has 30 LEDs that can reach 154 lumens with a 360 degree spread, and you adjust the brightness by changing how far you extend it. It is battery powered and comes as a pair, which is useful for a bedroom and a bathroom.

The tradeoff is brightness. At 154 lumens it is bright enough for a table or a hallway but not for a large room. The listing does not detail the battery type or runtime in what we saw, so check before buying. A telescoping body is also more delicate than a solid lantern.

For ownership, it stores in a drawer and sets up in seconds. Compared with the Consciot it is far smaller and lighter, and compared with plug in lights it needs to be switched on. It is a good second light for a bedside or a bathroom shelf.
products.bestFor: Bedside or bathroom use where a compact, dimmable lantern is welcome.

buyingCriteria.explanation: The most important question is whether the light turns on by itself. The ROSSEX and Energizer switch on automatically when power fails, the bulbs glow if the switch is on, and the Consciot and Etekcity need a button press. In a dark house, hunting for a switch is the worst part of an outage. Put an automatic light on the route you walk first, such as bedroom to bathroom.

buyingCriteria.criterion: Brightness and where you use it
buyingCriteria.explanation: Brightness should match the job. A guide light for a hallway needs only a modest glow, while a room light needs several hundred lumens. The DEBAOBULB lists 800 lumens on mains power, the Etekcity reaches 154 lumens and the Consciot claims 1000 lumens. Match the number to the space, and remember that brighter drains batteries faster.

An outage may last an hour or two days, so runtime matters. The BoRccdit claims up to 48 hours and offers 10, 50 and 100 percent levels, which is a flexible way to stretch power. Plug in lights rarely list runtimes, so assume them to be short term guides. Check the stated runtime at the level you will actually use.

Rechargeable plug ins and bulbs need no batteries, but they depend on being kept charged. The Consciot uses three D cells that must be bought and replaced. Choose a power source you will actually maintain. Check rechargeable units every few months so you know they still work.

Plug-in lights need an outlet, bulbs need the right socket and lanterns need a flat surface or hook. Bulbs like the DEBAOBULB use an E26 base, so check your fixtures and shade clearance. Plug ins like the Energizer take up outlet space. Walk your home and note where you would want light first.

Some lights double as a handheld torch, such as the Energizer and ROSSEX. Lanterns like the Etekcity and Consciot hang or stand. Weight and grip matter if you will carry it up stairs in the dark. A light you can hold with one hand while steadying yourself on a rail is a safer choice.

howWeEvaluated.title: Automatic activation
howWeEvaluated.description: We checked how each light starts. The ROSSEX and Energizer are designed to come on when power fails, the bulbs stay lit if their switch is on, and the lanterns require a button. We gave more credit to lights that need no action, because it matters most in the dark.

howWeEvaluated.title: Brightness and coverage
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared listed brightness: 800 lumens on mains for the DEBAOBULB, 154 lumens for the Etekcity, and a 1000 lumen claim for the Consciot. We noted that plug ins did not list brightness in the details we saw. These are all maker claims and were used to compare, not to rate.

howWeEvaluated.title: Runtime and power source
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at power source and runtime. The BoRccdit claims up to 48 hours with three levels, the Consciot uses three D cells, and the plug ins use built in rechargeable batteries. Where runtime was missing we said so and did not guess.

howWeEvaluated.title: Setup and upkeep
howWeEvaluated.description: A light that is hard to set up will go unused. We looked at plug in, screw in and carry designs, and at the need for batteries or regular recharging. Simple devices that need little attention earned credit for reliability.

howWeEvaluated.title: Lineup positioning and value
howWeEvaluated.description: The Energizer leads for simple plug in use, the ROSSEX for multi function packs, the DEBAOBULB for room lighting, the BoRccdit for long backup claims, the Consciot for brightness and the Etekcity for compact portability. Value is the fit between a light's strengths and where you need it.

howToChoose.intro: Place lights by route and room, not by gadget.
howToChoose.note: Walk through your home in the dark once and mark where you would want a light.

howToChoose.intro: The central tradeoff is automatic versus portable.

cards.label: Plug-in lights
cards.text: The ROSSEX and Energizer sit in outlets, stay charged and turn on by themselves. They are ideal for the first moments and for guiding you on a route. They are small lights, not room lights. Choose them for hallways, stairs and bedrooms.

cards.label: Battery lanterns
cards.text: The Consciot and Etekcity are carried where you need them and light a whole table or room. They need a button press and fresh batteries. Choose them for long outages and for sitting areas.

howToChoose.intro: A second axis is whether to use your own fixtures.
howToChoose.note: Remember that bulbs need the wall switch on.

howToChoose.intro: Most outage accidents happen on the way to the bathroom.

cards.label: Look for
cards.text: Look for a light that comes on without you doing anything and lights the floor. Put one near the bed, one in the hall and one at the top and bottom of the stairs. Keep a handheld light on the nightstand. Check the batteries on a schedule.

cards.label: In this comparison
cards.text: The ROSSEX 4-in-1 Plug-In Emergency Light is a nightlight every day and an emergency light when needed. The Energizer Weatheready Auto-On LED Light 3-Pack lifts out as a handheld. The Etekcity lantern is a good bedside backup.

howToChoose.note: Ask a doctor or occupational therapist about home safety if mobility is a concern.

howToChoose.intro: Spend on coverage, not on brightness you will not use.

faq.q: What is the best way to prepare for a power outage?
faq.a: Use a layered approach: plug in auto-on lights on your main routes, a lantern for sitting areas and a handheld light by the bed. Check them every few months. This covers the first seconds and the long evening.

faq.q: How bright should an emergency light be?
faq.a: Around 20 to 40 lumens is enough to guide you through a hallway or bathroom, and a room feels lit at about 80 lumens or more. The Etekcity reaches 154 lumens and the DEBAOBULB lists 800 on mains power. Brighter lights drain batteries faster.

faq.q: How long do emergency lights last?
faq.a: It varies by model and brightness. The BoRccdit claims up to 48 hours at its lowest level. Many plug ins do not list a runtime, so treat them as short term guides.

faq.q: Do rechargeable bulbs work as regular bulbs?
faq.a: Yes. The DEBAOBULB and BoRccdit work in standard sockets when mains power is on, and recharge themselves. In an outage they stay lit if the switch is on.

faq.q: Are these lights code-compliant exit lights?
faq.a: No claim of that kind is made on these listings, so do not use them as commercial exit lighting. They are home preparedness lights. For a building that needs code compliant lighting, consult a qualified electrician.

faq.q: How do I keep them ready?
faq.a: Test plug in lights by unplugging them occasionally, and recharge or replace batteries on a schedule. Store lanterns with fresh batteries. A light that has not been checked in a year is not a plan.
